item.title: Bernstein halves Nvidia target to $200, the 3rd broker in 2 days to step back over Huang
item.description:
Three brokers stepping back in two days removes an important source of support for Nvidia, just as the stock heads into results. Bernstein’s method matters for the wider AI trade. By cutting the multiple rather than earnings, it frames the problem as risk specific to Nvidia, not a slowdown in AI demand. That supports the rotation seen after hours, with AMD, Broadcom and Alphabet benefiting. For the indexes, Nvidia falling below a $4 trillion valuation would weigh heavily on the S&P 500 and Nasdaq. Futures and the Asian chip supply chain are likely to stay sensitive to any board announcement before November 17.

---

Bernstein still believes in Nvidia’s chips, just not in paying 25 times earnings while nobody knows who will be running the company.

Summary:

  • Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon downgraded Nvidia to Market Perform from Outperform and cut his target to $200 from $400
  • He said leadership uncertainty, not weak chip sales, drove the move, and that Bernstein may not yet fully understand how deep the issue goes
  • Rasgon kept earnings forecasts unchanged, saying AI demand remains very strong, but halved the valuation multiple to about 12.7x fiscal 2028 earnings
  • Morgan Stanley stepped back on November 11, and Baird cut Nvidia to Neutral with a $200 target, down from $500
  • Nvidia fell roughly 8% after hours to around $160, on track to drop below a $4 trillion valuation

Bernstein has downgraded Nvidia to Market Perform from Outperform and halved its price target to $200 from $400. That makes it the third major brokerage in two days to step back from the stock as uncertainty over chief executive Jensen Huang’s future deepens.

Analyst Stacy Rasgon was clear that the move had nothing to do with weak chip sales. In a client note and a later CNBC appearance, he said the downgrade was driven by leadership uncertainty, after reports that Nvidia’s board is preparing to remove Huang, who has acknowledged an extramarital affair. Rasgon wrote that Bernstein’s instinct is that it may not yet fully understand how deep the issue goes, and that it has chosen to step back to the sidelines for now. He also told CNBC that replacing Huang would be very difficult, and that it is not obvious who could succeed him.

The way Bernstein cut its target is the most telling part of the call. Rasgon kept his earnings forecasts unchanged, saying underlying AI demand remains very strong. Instead, he halved the valuation multiple he is willing to pay. The new $200 target equals roughly 12.7 times consensus earnings of about $15.75 a share for the fiscal year ending January 2028, down from about 25.4 times at the old $400 target. In Bernstein’s view, the business has not changed. What has changed is the price investors should pay for its future earnings, because of the risk around who will run it.

Bernstein is not alone. Morgan Stanley stepped back on November 11. Baird downgraded Nvidia to Neutral from Outperform and also cut its target to $200, from $500, citing uncertainty over Huang’s future as well as concerns about supply and visibility on 2027 spending.

Nvidia shares fell roughly 8% in after-hours trading to around $160, putting the company on track to slip below a $4 trillion market value. The drop pulled down AI infrastructure names such as CoreWeave and Super Micro Computer.

Even at $200, Bernstein’s target sits above where the shares are trading after hours, which suggests the bank sees the risk as uncertainty rather than collapse. The next markers are any board decision on Huang and Nvidia’s third-quarter results on November 17, when management will face questions on both demand and leadership.

item.title: CBA’s Chambers sees room for higher US 10-year yields despite the slide in oil prices
item.description:
A further rise in the 10-year yield toward and beyond 5% would keep the dollar supported. That matters most for USD/JPY, which is already near the 160 area where Japan has stepped up verbal warnings. Higher long-end yields would also weigh on gold, which has slipped below $4,000, and add pressure on richly valued tech stocks already hit by the Nvidia leadership shock. Oil is the key risk to the call. A sustained fall in crude would ease inflation fears and could cap yields, while a renewed rise linked to the Iran war would reinforce the move higher.

---

Cheaper oil might give Treasuries a breather, but CBA thinks growth and a hawkish Fed will keep pushing the 10-year yield higher.

Summary:

  • CBA’s Chambers says US Treasury yields have room to rise further
  • Yields jumped after a hot October CPI report and hawkish comments from Fed officials
  • Markets have largely priced in a December Fed hike
  • A sharp fall in oil prices may temporarily halt the rise in yields over the coming weeks
  • Chambers expects economic momentum and firmer Fed hike expectations to dominate, pushing the 10-year yield higher

US Treasury yields have further room to rise, even if the recent slide in oil prices slows their advance in the coming weeks, according to Commonwealth Bank of Australia rates strategist Chambers.

Yields have climbed sharply this week. A hotter than expected October inflation report, with consumer prices up 0.4% on the month and core prices up 0.3%, pushed the 10-year yield up 11 basis points to close to 5% on Tuesday. Hawkish comments from Federal Reserve officials added to the move. Governor Christopher Waller raised the idea of a 50 basis point hike in December, and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said she favors at least two more quarter-point increases. Markets have largely priced in a December hike.

Chambers is watching two forces pulling in opposite directions. Oil prices have dropped sharply, which eases inflation concerns and could act as a temporary brake on yields. But he expects economic momentum and firmer expectations of Fed tightening to win out, pushing the 10-year yield higher in the near term.

That view fits a broader shift in bank forecasts this week. Deutsche Bank now expects quarter-point Fed hikes in December, January and March, while UBS sees hikes in December and March and has flagged the risk of a faster pace. If more forecasters move toward back-to-back hikes, longer-dated yields would have to adjust higher to reflect a higher expected path for policy.

Oil remains the main risk to the call. Crude has been volatile. Brent dipped below $90 a barrel earlier this week, then rebounded as attacks on shipping continued during the Iran war. A sustained fall in energy prices would weaken the inflation argument for further hikes, while a renewed spike would strengthen it.

For now, the balance looks tilted toward higher yields. That would keep the dollar supported and add pressure on assets that are sensitive to rates, from gold to richly valued technology stocks.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ANZ says RBA hike bets have cooled, but 3.7% core inflation will keep it cautious
item.description:
Cooler RBA hike expectations take away one source of support for the Australian dollar, at a time when US yields are rising and the Fed is on a hiking path. That leaves the AUD exposed to further dollar strength. Sticky services inflation should limit how far Australian rate expectations can fall, though, which caps the downside for front-end bond yields. Lower oil prices help Australian headline inflation but do little for the domestic services pressures ANZ is focused on, so the RBA’s cautious stance looks likely to persist.

---

Growth is cooling, but services inflation isn’t, and that keeps the RBA from relaxing even as the case for another hike fades.

Summary:

  • ANZ economist Siddhant Kalra says expectations of further RBA rate hikes have cooled as Australia’s economy slows
  • Q3 trimmed mean inflation rose 1.0% q/q and 3.7% y/y, above forecasts and above the RBA’s 2% to 3% target band
  • Market services inflation posted its strongest annual gain since 2024
  • ANZ links market services prices to domestic capacity pressures
  • It says the strong result will keep the RBA cautious in the coming months

Expectations of further interest rate increases by the Reserve Bank of Australia have cooled as signs mount that the economy is slowing. But persistent inflation means the central bank is unlikely to drop its guard, according to ANZ economist Siddhant Kalra.

The pressure shows up most clearly in the RBA’s preferred core measure. The trimmed mean, which strips out the most extreme price moves each quarter, rose 1.0% in the third quarter and 3.7% from a year earlier. That was above forecasts and above the top of the central bank’s 2% to 3% target band. Market services inflation, which covers prices that depend mainly on local demand and labor costs, posted its strongest annual increase since 2024.

Kalra highlighted the services detail as the key point. Market services prices are closely linked to domestic capacity pressures, so they reflect how stretched the Australian economy is, rather than global influences such as oil prices or the currency. A strong reading suggests demand is still running up against the economy’s limits, which is the kind of inflation central banks find hardest to bring down.

ANZ said the strength of the result is likely to keep the RBA cautious in the coming months. That leaves the bank in an awkward position. Slowing growth argues against more tightening, while sticky underlying inflation argues against signaling that rates have peaked, let alone opening the door to cuts.

The global backdrop adds to the tension. Lower oil prices are easing pressure on headline inflation, but central banks elsewhere are leaning hawkish. The US Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise rates in December after a hotter than expected October inflation report, and the Bank of Japan is also expected to hike.

For the RBA, the coming months are likely to be about patience rather than action. Unless services inflation eases, a meaningful shift toward lower rates looks some way off, even if the bar for another hike has risen. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Deutsche Bank sees 3 straight Fed hikes after hot CPI, adding a January move
item.description:
A no-pause path into March is more hawkish than markets have priced beyond December. If other banks follow, it would likely be repriced through the front end of the Treasury curve and the dollar. That keeps USD/JPY pressed toward the 160 area where Tokyo is already warning, and it adds to the headwinds for gold. For equities, a faster sequence of hikes lands at an awkward moment, with AI stocks already under pressure from the Nvidia leadership shock. Oil remains the wildcard: renewed energy-driven inflation would strengthen the case for back-to-back hikes, while a sustained easing in crude would weaken it.

---

Deutsche Bank has turned UBS’s “faster tightening” risk into its base case, and the Fed debate is now about the pace after December, not whether December happens.

Summary:

  • Deutsche Bank now expects 25bp Fed hikes in December, January and March, adding a January move to its previous December and March path
  • That would lift the federal funds target range to 4.50% to 4.75%, from 3.75% to 4% now
  • The revision followed October CPI, which rose 0.4% m/m against a 0.3% forecast, and which the bank said showed broad-based gains
  • Deutsche Bank won’t rule out a 50bp December hike after Waller’s comments, but it isn’t the bank’s base case
  • UBS keeps a base case of hikes in December and March only
  • Markets price a December quarter-point hike at more than 95%, according to CME FedWatch

Deutsche Bank now expects the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at each of its next three meetings, after adding a January increase to its forecast following a hotter than expected US inflation report. The bank sees quarter-point hikes in December, January and March. That would lift the federal funds target range to 4.50% to 4.75%, from 3.75% to 4% now.

Deutsche Bank had previously expected hikes in December and March, with a pause in January. The October consumer price report changed that view. Headline prices rose 0.4% on the month against forecasts of 0.3%, and the bank said the data continued to show broad-based gains.

The bank also addressed the idea of a larger move. Before the data, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a 50 basis point hike should be considered in December if price pressures accelerated, and Deutsche Bank said his comments opened that possibility. It would not rule out a half-point increase, but said a 50 basis point move is not its base case.

The revision puts Deutsche Bank at the more hawkish end of the major banks. UBS, for example, said this week it sees limited support on the rate-setting committee for a 50 basis point step. It keeps a base case of quarter-point hikes in December and March only, although it flagged the risk of more or faster tightening. The two views share a common thread: the debate has shifted from whether the Fed hikes in December to how quickly it follows through.

Markets are close to fully pricing a December move. Traders put the odds of a quarter-point hike at the December 8-9 meeting above 95%, according to CME FedWatch.

The path matters well beyond bonds. Three consecutive hikes would keep pressure on Treasury yields, which climbed close to 5% after the CPI release, and would support the dollar. It also raises the bar for assets that have struggled with higher rates, from gold, which has slipped back below $4,000 an ounce, to richly valued technology stocks. The next tests come from November’s labor market data and further Fed commentary before the December meeting. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: 5 forced sellers that can turn a market dip into a rout, and how to spot them
item.description:
This framework is directly relevant now. Tonight’s Nvidia slide hits one of the most widely held stocks among hedge funds, and futures are lower ahead of the cash session. If volatility jumps again, the same mechanical sellers (volatility-control funds, leveraged ETFs and options dealers) could amplify the move into the US close, especially in crowded AI names. The signals worth watching are credit spreads, Treasury behavior and whether selling spreads beyond the AI complex. With 10-year yields close to 5% after a hot CPI, bonds are not currently offering much of a hedge, which is one of the conditions that makes a positioning shake-out harder to absorb.

-- Not every sharp fall is a verdict on fundamentals. Sometimes it’s just leveraged investors following their rules, and knowing who has to sell helps you judge whether a sell-off will last.

Summary:

  • Sharp market declines are often amplified by investors who are forced to sell, not by investors who have changed their view
  • Leverage creates a feedback loop, because losses force sales that push prices lower and trigger more forced selling
  • The main mechanical sellers are volatility-control funds, CTAs, leveraged ETFs, options dealers and crowded leveraged hedge funds
  • Last week’s 6.4% Nasdaq-100 drop saw an estimated record $56 billion of leveraged ETF selling, with a potential $61 billion more from volatility-control funds
  • Signs of a positioning-driven sell-off include stable earnings forecasts, contained credit spreads and losses concentrated in crowded stocks
  • This piece expands on an analysis by Saxo investment strategist Victoria Ramirez

When markets fall hard, it’s natural to assume investors have suddenly changed their minds about the economy or a company’s prospects. Often the bigger driver is simpler: a group of investors who have no choice but to sell. Understanding who they are, and why their selling arrives when it does, helps explain why some declines snowball while others fade quickly.

This explainer builds on a very good analysis by Saxo investment strategist Victoria Ramirez, reworked here with added explanation for readers newer to market mechanics. Her starting point is last week’s slide in US technology shares. The Nasdaq-100 fell 6.4% in a single session, its worst day since March 2020, wiping roughly $2.3 trillion off the market’s value. Concerns over AI data center spending started the move, but mechanical selling by systematic and leveraged investors turned it into a broad, indiscriminate decline.

The key is leverage. Imagine a fund that invests $200 in shares, using $100 of its own money and $100 borrowed. If those shares fall 10%, the portfolio drops to $180, but the debt is unchanged. The fund’s own capital has therefore shrunk from $100 to $80, a 20% loss. To get back to its original leverage, it can now only hold $160 of shares, so it has to sell $20, after prices have already fallen. Those sales push prices lower, which can force the next leveraged investor to do the same. 

Several types of investor follow rules like this:

  • Volatility-control funds keep the risk in their portfolios steady. When market swings double, they roughly halve their exposure.
  • Trend-following funds, often called CTAs, cut positions when prices break below key trend levels, and they may keep selling for days after the original news.
  • Leveraged ETFs rebalance every day, so a big down day forces them to sell into the close.
  • Options dealers who have sold protection to investors may need to sell more of the market as it falls, to stay hedged.
  • Leveraged hedge funds that crowd into the same popular stocks can be forced to dump them together when lenders demand more collateral.

The scale can be large. Saxo cites estimates that leveraged ETF rebalancing removed about $56 billion of equity exposure on November 5, a record according to Nomura’s model. Volatility-control funds faced potential selling of around $61 billion, and trend followers sold about $13 billion of US index futures. Those sums are only a few percent of a day’s trading. But because prices are set at the margin, a small amount of urgent, one-way selling can move the whole market.

The practical lesson is that a sharp fall is not always a verdict on fundamentals. Signs that a sell-off is mainly about positioning include:

  • stable earnings forecasts
  • only modest widening in credit spreads
  • normal conditions in funding markets
  • government bonds acting as a hedge again
  • losses concentrated in previously crowded or expensive stocks

When those hold, prices have often recovered once the forced selling ends.

That isn’t guaranteed. If one of those signals breaks, such as credit markets seizing up or bonds falling alongside stocks, a positioning shake-out can turn into something more serious. Knowing who is selling, and why, helps investors judge which kind of sell-off they are facing. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ICYMI: OPEC output jumps nearly 2 million bpd toward prewar levels as Saudi production rebounds
item.description:
The supply recovery takes some of the edge off shortage fears and helps explain why Brent dipped below $90 earlier this week. But the rebound in prices on Wednesday shows that the war risk premium is far from gone. With confirmed Hormuz transits still a fraction of normal, any escalation that hits pipelines or Red Sea routes would quickly reverse the gains in supply. Aramco’s deeper discount to Asia points to weaker pricing power for Gulf crude and is a modest positive for Asian refiners. For the wider macro picture, oil remains the main channel through which the war feeds inflation. Steadier supply would ease pressure on the Fed and the BoJ, while renewed disruption would harden the case for further hikes.

-

OPEC has found ways around the Strait of Hormuz, but with transits through the strait still about a quarter of normal, supply is recovering on workarounds, not on peace.

Summary:

  • OPEC crude output rose by nearly 2 million bpd in October to about 27.2 million bpd, against about 28.6 million before the Iran war, The Wall Street Journal (gated) reported, citing OPEC data
  • Saudi Arabia raised production to around 10.6 million bpd from about 8.4 million in September
  • Pipelines, ship-to-ship transfers and US military support have helped Gulf producers sustain exports
  • Confirmed Hormuz transits averaged about 4 million bpd last week, compared with roughly 17 million before the war, according to Kpler
  • Saudi Aramco cut December Arab Light prices to Asia by $2 a barrel to a $7 discount to Oman/Dubai
  • Brent rose 1.5% to around $93 on Wednesday, and OPEC left its demand forecasts unchanged

OPEC’s crude production climbed back toward prewar levels in October, with Saudi Arabia leading a sharp rebound, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing OPEC’s latest monthly data. Alternative pipelines, ship-to-ship transfers and other workarounds allowed Gulf producers to keep oil flowing despite continued attacks on shipping.

Output from the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries rose by nearly 2 million barrels a day to about 27.2 million barrels a day last month. That compares with about 28.6 million in February, before the Iran war began. Saudi Arabia, the group’s de facto leader, raised production to around 10.6 million barrels a day from about 8.4 million in September.

More than eight months into the conflict, US military support, tanker-to-tanker transfers and cross-country pipelines have helped producers sustain exports. They have done so even as vessels in the Strait of Hormuz face repeated attacks and the Houthis threaten Red Sea traffic. Saudi crude exports averaged around 7 million barrels a day in October, according to Kpler data. That was slightly lower than September but still above the kingdom’s 2025 average of about 6.2 million. Loadings from Saudi Arabia’s eastern terminals on the Gulf coast have picked up again, after exports shifted toward Red Sea ports earlier in the war.

The strait itself remains the bottleneck. Before the war, it carried around a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas. Confirmed transits averaged about 4 million barrels a day over the past week, compared with roughly 17 million before the conflict, Kpler data show. Those figures are preliminary, though, and some tankers cross with their transponders switched off.

Gulf producers are discounting heavily to win buyers and offset high tanker and freight costs. Saudi Aramco cut its December official selling price for Arab Light crude to Asia by $2 a barrel, to a $7 discount to the Oman/Dubai benchmark.

The data arrived as oil prices rebounded. Brent rose 1.5% to around $93 a barrel on Wednesday, after dipping below $90 earlier in the week. West Texas Intermediate gained 1.6% to about $87. Ongoing attacks and uncertainty over US-Iran peace talks tempered hopes of de-escalation.

OPEC kept its demand forecasts unchanged. It expects global consumption to rise by 180,000 barrels a day this year and 2.55 million barrels a day next year. Key OPEC+ members agreed earlier this month to hold output steady in December. The recovery in supply eases the worst of the shortage fears. But with Hormuz flows still a fraction of normal, the market remains exposed to any fresh disruption. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BoJ’s Asada, who opposed 2 hikes this year, urges caution on pace as rates near neutral
item.description:
Asada’s views are well known, so the speech is unlikely to change December pricing much. A December hike is still the consensus, and a single dissent would not block it. The timing matters for the yen, though. A dovish voice from the board, on the same morning that officials are warning about rapid moves with USD/JPY near 160, gives yen bears a talking point and makes Tokyo’s verbal defense harder. For Japanese government bonds, his emphasis on caution supports the view that any hikes beyond December will be gradual, which could cap yields at the front end. With oil-driven input costs still pushing producer prices up, though, the hawks on the board hold the stronger hand for now.

---

Asada isn’t trying to stop a December hike so much as put the brakes on what comes after it, arguing that with rates near neutral, every further move carries more risk.

Summary:

  • BoJ board member Toichiro Asada urged due consideration of the pace of further rate hikes in a speech in Nagasaki
  • He voted against the June and September hikes, which took the policy rate to 1.25%
  • With the policy rate already inside the BoJ’s estimated neutral range of slightly above 1% to 2.5%, he sees growing risks to the economy from further tightening
  • He said consumption is more or less flat and recent price gains are not necessarily driven by demand
  • He sees further hikes as more likely when higher wages spur demand-driven inflation
  • He acknowledged high profits, a tight labor market, positive real wages and producer price inflation of around 7%

Bank of Japan board member Toichiro Asada urged caution on the pace of further interest rate increases on Thursday. He argued that with policy already inside the estimated neutral range, each additional hike carries a growing risk of slowing the economy. The remarks, in a speech to local leaders in Nagasaki, mark him once again as one of the board’s most dovish voices ahead of the December meeting, where most economists expect a hike.

Asada voted against both of this year’s rate increases, in June and September, which took the policy rate to 1.25%, the highest in around three decades. He said the Bank estimates the neutral interest rate, the level that neither stimulates nor restrains the economy, at roughly slightly above 1% to 2.5%. With the policy rate already in that range, he argued that monetary accommodation is gradually diminishing and that further hikes are more likely to hurt activity than when the tightening cycle began. He added that it can take a year or more for the effect of a rate increase to become clear.

His central concern is consumption. The Bank officially describes private spending as resilient, but Asada said it has been more or less flat and is not strong enough to drive overall growth. In his view, recent price gains have not necessarily been driven by demand. He said any further hike would most likely come when higher wages spur demand-driven inflation, and that the Bank should give due consideration to the pace of tightening.

He did acknowledge strength elsewhere. Corporate profits are high, supported by global AI-related demand. Unemployment is around 2.5%, base pay rises have held up for a third year, and real wages have been positive since the start of 2026. He also noted that producer price inflation has been running at around 7%, and said the key question is how quickly cost pressures further up the supply chain reach consumers. Core consumer inflation is around 2%, held down by government energy subsidies, although a measure that excludes such institutional factors is running at 3% to 3.5%.

Asada’s speech came on the same morning that data showed Japan’s producer prices rising a faster than expected 7.1% in October. Finance ministry officials were also warning against rapid yen moves, with USD/JPY near 160. Those pressures strengthen the case for the majority on the board. A single dissent would not block a December hike, but it would underline that the board’s appetite for a faster pace of tightening is limited. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Google TPUs could gain share from Nvidia turmoil, Bloomberg Intelligence says, eyeing $50B
item.description:
The Huang uncertainty is turning Nvidia’s reliance on a single leader into a selling point for its rivals. Alphabet and AMD are the clearest beneficiaries, at least in sentiment. Any sign that customers are actually moving spending, rather than just talking about it, would matter for the AI hardware supply chain, including Asian suppliers whose fortunes are tied closely to Nvidia’s volumes. A diversification story also supports the case for Google Cloud’s growth multiple. For now, though, the trade is driven by headlines, and a clean leadership outcome or strong results from Nvidia on November 17 could quickly reverse the relative moves.

--

Nvidia’s crisis at the top gives Google a rare opening to pitch its cheaper AI chips, but CUDA lock-in means any shift in spending would take years, not days.

Summary:

  • Bloomberg Intelligence says Google’s TPUs could gain share if Nvidia’s leadership uncertainty pushes customers to diversify toward lower-priced chips
  • A wider rollout of Google’s 8tx and 8i Max chips would extend its reach across AI training and inference
  • Hyperscalers and frontier AI labs could lean more heavily on non-Nvidia chips as a result
  • TPU systems were a meaningful contributor to Google Cloud in the third quarter, and TPU sales are seen ramping to more than $50 billion in 2027
  • The note follows a WSJ report that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang, which sent Nvidia shares down more than 10% after hours

Google’s tensor processing units could pick up market share if the turmoil around Nvidia’s leadership encourages AI customers to spread their spending across more chip suppliers, according to Bloomberg Intelligence. The research arm said a wider rollout of Google’s expanded TPU lineup could lead hyperscalers and frontier AI labs to lean more heavily on non-Nvidia chips. It expects TPU sales to ramp to more than $50 billion in 2027.

The note comes as Nvidia faces the most serious leadership uncertainty in its history. The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that the company’s board is preparing to oust chief executive Jensen Huang. That followed a New York Times report of a relationship with an executive who reports to him, on top of an existing board investigation into his ties to a businesswoman whom US officials identified as a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia shares fell more than 10% in after-hours trading, while rival chipmaker AMD rose.

Bloomberg Intelligence’s argument rests on price and timing. TPUs are typically cheaper than Nvidia’s graphics processors, and customers worried about their supply relationships or the continuity of Nvidia’s product plans may see this as a moment to diversify. A broader rollout of Google’s newer chips, which the research arm identified as the 8tx and 8i Max, would extend Google’s reach across both training, where AI models are built, and inference, where they are run for users.

The financial stakes are significant for Alphabet. TPU systems were already a meaningful contributor to Google Cloud sales in the third quarter, the research arm said, and faster adoption would support further growth in the division.

There are limits to the argument. Nvidia’s lead rests on more than its chief executive. Its CUDA software platform, which most AI developers are trained on, makes switching costly. Large AI buyers also plan their chip purchases years ahead, so any shift in spending would likely be gradual rather than sudden. And leadership uncertainty does not change Nvidia’s products overnight.

The next test comes quickly. Nvidia reports third-quarter results on November 17, and any comment on customer demand, the board’s review or succession will show whether the uncertainty is affecting orders. For Google, the question is whether it can turn interest in TPUs into firm commitments while its biggest rival is distracted. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: TD Securities sees gold retesting $3,900 as Fed hike bets and a firm dollar bite
item.description:
With a December Fed hike close to fully priced, gold’s next leg depends on whether markets start to price a faster sequence of hikes. That makes Fed speakers and next month’s data more important for bullion than geopolitical headlines. A firmer dollar, helped by Treasury yields near 5%, adds to the pressure, especially as Japan’s attempts to slow the yen’s slide (which continued today) have so far done little to dent broad dollar strength. On the downside, central bank buying below $4,000 may cushion the fall. On the upside, any sign that oil prices are easing would weaken the inflation case for further hikes and could quickly revive interest in gold.

-

TD’s $3,900 floor once looked safe as long as the Fed held off, but with hikes back on the table, the bank now expects it to be tested.

Summary:

  • TD Securities’ Bart Melek expects gold to retest support near $3,900 an ounce, citing higher US rates and a stronger dollar
  • Gold slipped below $4,000 on Wednesday, extending a two-day slide after hotter than expected US October CPI
  • In July, TD said a break below $3,900 was unlikely unless the Fed hiked early, and that condition has now flipped
  • TD described gold as range-bound between $3,900 and $4,250 in late October
  • The bank still sees potential for record highs above $5,300 in 2027 once oil-driven inflation fades
  • Analysts flag $3,940 to $4,000 as a key zone, with central bank buying tending to pick up below $4,000

Gold is likely to retest support near $3,900 an ounce as rising US interest rates and a stronger dollar keep weighing on investment demand, according to TD Securities. In a report published on Tuesday, Bart Melek, the bank’s head of commodity strategy, said the pressure on the metal has further to run before the longer-term bull case can return.

The call came as gold slipped below $4,000 an ounce on Wednesday. That extended a two-day decline after October’s US inflation report came in hotter than expected and cemented bets that the Federal Reserve will raise rates in December. Higher rates raise the opportunity cost of holding gold, which pays no yield. A firmer dollar makes it more expensive for buyers using other currencies.

The note marks a clear shift in TD’s thinking since mid-year. In early July, Melek argued that a break below $3,900 was unlikely as long as an early Fed rate hike remained off the table. That condition no longer holds. With the Fed on a hiking path and futures fully pricing a December move, the floor TD once saw as secure is now the level it expects to be tested. As recently as late October, the bank described gold as stuck in a range between $3,900 and $4,250.

Gold’s recent behavior reinforces the point. item.title: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights: 3 reasons it matters beyond travel
item.description:
This is a small story for United’s earnings, but a meaningful signal for the AI monetisation theme. Agentic commerce, where AI tools buy on a user’s behalf, is one of the main ways AI developers hope to turn assistants into revenue. Every large merchant that limits agents to browsing makes that harder. The timing matters, with Nvidia’s results and Anthropic’s market debut both due next week and investors already testing how much AI revenue current valuations assume. If restrictions spread across airlines, retail and banking, merchants with strong direct channels would protect their customer data, pricing power and advertising reach, while AI platforms would be pushed toward partnership deals rather than open access.

---

United will let AI agents window-shop but not buy, and if other big merchants follow, the business case for agentic commerce gets a lot harder.

Summary:

  • United Airlines will stop personal AI assistants from booking tickets through its systems, The Wall Street Journal (gated) reported
  • The airline cited the risk of exposing customer data, unintended purchases, and possible breaches of FAA and Transportation Department rules
  • AI agents can still show United’s flights and fares but cannot transact on its website
  • CEO Scott Kirby said he does not want to create another middleman
  • Delta and American allow some agent bookings, while Amazon has also moved to keep shopping bots away
  • Agent volumes remain tiny: Uber said AI agents made just four ride bookings and 500 Eats orders during Halloween week

United Airlines will stop personal AI assistants from booking tickets through its systems, the carrier said on Wednesday, according to The Wall Street Journal. It is the first major US airline to publicly push back against so-called agentic commerce, in which AI tools act on a customer’s behalf rather than just answering questions.

United gave three reasons. Third-party agents could expose customers’ sensitive information. They could make purchases customers did not intend. And automated actions could breach Federal Aviation Administration and Transportation Department rules on what airlines must show passengers. For example, an AI agent cannot confirm at check-in that a bag contains no explosives. Agents will still be able to display United’s flights and fares, but they will not be able to complete transactions on its website.

There is also a commercial motive. Chief executive Scott Kirby, who has called AI potentially transformational, said on Tuesday that he does not want to create another middleman. Airlines spent years fighting online travel agencies over how their fares were displayed and sold. An AI agent that compares prices and books on a customer’s behalf could weaken the direct relationship carriers have worked hard to win back.

United is not alone. Amazon sued Perplexity in November 2025 to stop its Comet browser agent from shopping on Amazon’s site, and later won a court order that temporarily blocked it. Other airlines are taking a different line. Delta lets authenticated AI assistants complete bookings, with extra safeguards for sensitive trips such as those involving unaccompanied minors. American says some agents can buy tickets through certain partners.

For now the volumes are tiny. United said it is not seeing many bookings from agents. Uber said that over Halloween week, AI agents accounted for just 500 Uber Eats orders and four rides, out of about 320 million trips. The bigger question is what happens if more large merchants follow United and Amazon. AI developers are betting that agents will become a new way to buy things. They include OpenAI, which this week bought travel-booking startup Odessia, and Meta, which says travel planning is a top use for its Muse agent. If major sellers keep agents at the browsing stage, that route to making money from AI gets narrower, and the companies that own the customer relationship keep the upper hand.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6797 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan’s Mimura warns yen moves are too rapid as USD/JPY pushes back toward 160
item.description:
Japan’s 2026 track record means USD/JPY near 160 now carries real two-way risk, and that should make traders more reluctant to chase fresh highs even if the trend stays up. The bigger driver remains the US-Japan rate gap. A Fed on a hiking path and 10-year Treasury yields close to 5% keep the dollar supported, which limits how far warnings alone can push the pair lower. A firmer escalation in official language, or signs of US backing like the joint operation in the summer, would raise the odds of a sharp drop in USD/JPY. A weak yen also amplifies the cost of imported oil, keeping pressure on the Bank of Japan ahead of its December meeting.

Newswire cut: Japan’s vice finance minister for international affairs Atsushi Mimura said recent currency moves, including those of the past few days, are too rapid, as USD/JPY climbed back toward 160, the level that drew yen-buying intervention twice this year.

One-line wrap: Tokyo has started its familiar warning sequence on the yen, and with intervention twice this year above 160, markets have reason to listen, even if US yields are still pulling the other way.

Summary:

  • Japan’s Atsushi Mimura said currency moves, including those over the past few days, are too rapid
  • His remarks came as USD/JPY climbed back toward 160
  • Japan intervened to buy yen around late April and early May, and again in late July in a joint operation with the United States
  • The yen has been pressured by a hot US CPI report and Treasury yields close to 5%
  • That has offset Japan’s stronger than expected 7.1% producer price reading and expectations of a BoJ hike in December
  • Traders are watching for stronger official language, such as promises of “decisive action”

Main article: Japan stepped up its verbal defense of the yen on Thursday. Atsushi Mimura, vice finance minister for international affairs, said currency moves over the past few days have been too rapid. The comments came as USD/JPY climbed back toward 160, a level that has twice this year preceded actual intervention by Japanese authorities.

Mimura, who oversees Japan’s currency policy, spoke at around 00:13 GMT (19:13 US Eastern). His focus on the speed of the move is the standard first step in Tokyo’s warning sequence. Officials typically escalate from describing moves as rapid or excessive, to saying they are watching with a strong sense of urgency, and then to promising decisive action. In 2026, that kind of language has preceded both interventions.

That track record gives the warning weight. Japan carried out its largest-ever yen-buying intervention around the Golden Week holidays in late April and early May, after the dollar rose above 160. In late July, with the pair again above that level, Tokyo intervened once more. In early August, Japan and the United States confirmed that operation had been carried out jointly, the first coordinated yen-buying since the 1998 Asian financial crisis.

The latest slide in the yen has been driven by the rate gap. A stronger than expected US inflation report this week reinforced expectations of a Federal Reserve hike in December and pushed the 10-year Treasury yield close to 5%. That has outweighed strong data at home. Japan’s producer prices rose 7.1% in October from a year earlier, beating forecasts, and the Bank of Japan is widely expected to raise its 1.25% policy rate in December.

A weak yen also feeds directly into Japan’s inflation problem. Yen-based import prices are up nearly 25% from a year ago, led by oil, so further weakness in the currency raises costs for companies and households.

For traders, the near-term question is whether officials escalate their language. If USD/JPY breaks decisively above 160 and the rhetoric shifts toward decisive action, the risk of another intervention rises sharply. Until then, verbal warnings tend to slow the move rather than reverse it, especially while US yields keep rising.

item.title: Japan wholesale inflation speeds up to 7.1%, beating forecasts and firming BoJ hike bets
item.description:
The upside surprise adds to the case for a Bank of Japan hike in December. It should give the yen some support at the margin, although a Fed that is also on a hiking path after a hot US CPI limits how much the rate gap narrows. Oil is the key swing factor, because crude and fuel imports drove most of October’s import price jump. Any further rise in energy prices tied to the Iran war would feed directly into Japan’s pipeline inflation and strengthen the hawks’ argument. For Japanese government bonds, a firmer inflation backdrop keeps upward pressure on yields. For equities, rising input costs are a risk to margins for manufacturers that cannot pass them on.

---

Cheap rice is masking it, but energy, materials and a weak yen are pushing Japan’s pipeline inflation higher again, and that leaves little reason for the BoJ to wait.

Summary:

  • Japan’s corporate goods price index rose 7.1% y/y in October, above the 6.5% forecast and up from 6.8% in September
  • Prices rose 0.7% m/m against a 0.3% forecast, after a revised 0.2% decline in September
  • Petroleum and coal, chemicals, iron and steel, and utilities drove the gain, while lower rice prices dragged agriculture down 6.6% on the month
  • Yen-based import prices jumped 3.3% m/m and are up nearly 25% y/y, led by crude oil and fuels
  • The yen weakened about 1% over the month, adding to import costs
  • The data strengthen expectations of a Bank of Japan hike in December, after a hold at 1.25% in October

Japan’s wholesale inflation picked up again in October, as producer prices rose faster than forecast and added weight to expectations that the Bank of Japan will raise interest rates in December. The corporate goods price index rose 7.1% from a year earlier, Bank of Japan data showed on Thursday. That was above the 6.5% median forecast and up from 6.8% in September. On the month, prices climbed 0.7%, more than double the 0.3% expected, after a revised 0.2% decline in September.

The rebound ends two months of slowing in the annual rate, and it was driven mainly by energy and industrial materials. On the month, petroleum and coal products rose about 3%, chemicals about 2%, iron and steel 2%, and electricity, gas and water around 2.4%. Together, those four groups added roughly 0.6 percentage point to the monthly increase.

The headline would have been even stronger without food. Agricultural products fell 6.6% on the month and are down a quarter from a year ago, as cheaper newly harvested rice continues to drag on the index. Without that drag, the underlying push from manufactured goods and energy was close to a 1% monthly rise. That suggests pipeline pressure is spreading, not fading.

Import costs remain the main engine. The yen-based import price index jumped 3.3% in October and is nearly 25% higher than a year ago. Most of the monthly gain came from crude oil and other fuels, with energy imports up about 46% on the year in yen terms, as prices stay elevated during the Iran war. A 1% slide in the yen over the month added to the pressure. Imported memory chips and other electronics also rose sharply, echoing the firmness in technology goods prices seen elsewhere.

For the Bank of Japan, the data support a move at its December meeting. The central bank held its policy rate at 1.25% in late October in an 8-1 vote, with board member Hajime Takata pushing for an immediate hike. It also said underlying inflation had reached levels broadly consistent with its 2% target. A Bloomberg survey published before that meeting showed 83% of economists expecting a December increase.

Producer prices are an upstream gauge, and the BoJ places more weight on consumer inflation and wages. But with a weak yen and high oil prices, these costs are likely to keep feeding through to households, which makes a pause harder to justify.

---

October’s inflation report makes a December Fed hike look all but certain, and UBS thinks the real risk is a faster run of quarter-point moves rather than one big step.

Summary:

  • US October CPI rose 0.4% m/m (forecast 0.3%) and core rose 0.3% (forecast 0.2%), with broad price gains
  • The 10-year Treasury yield rose 11bp to close to 5% and the S&P 500 fell 0.4% on Tuesday
  • Fed Governor Waller said before the data that core at 0.3% or more could warrant considering a 50bp December hike, and Dallas Fed President Logan favors at least two more 25bp hikes
  • Fed funds futures price about 28bp of hikes for December
  • UBS sees limited FOMC support for 50bp and keeps its base case of 25bp hikes in December and March
  • Three-month annualized core inflation rose to about 3.75%, and tariff-sensitive and IT goods prices stayed firm

A hotter than expected US inflation report has put an unusual question in front of the Federal Reserve: whether its next hike should be a double-sized one. UBS thinks the answer is still no. But the bank says October’s data strengthen the case for at least two more quarter-point increases and raise the risk that they come faster.

Headline consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, above the 0.3% forecast. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3% against expectations of 0.2%. Price gains were broad, covering food, housing, recreation, medical care, electricity, airfares and delivery services. The 10-year Treasury yield jumped 11 basis points to close to 5%, and the S&P 500 fell 0.4% on Tuesday.

The 50 basis point idea came from Fed Governor Christopher Waller. Before the release, he said a core reading of around 0.3% or more could justify considering a half-point move in December.

  • Fed's Waller says a half-point rate hike in December may be needed if Core CPI comes in hot

Separately, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said she favors at least two more quarter-point hikes and suggested the Fed could move more quickly this winter.

  • Fed's Logan: It's clear that Fed needs at least two more quarter-point rate hikes

Fed funds futures now price about 28 basis points of tightening for December. That implies a full quarter-point hike and only a small chance of something larger.

UBS argues that appetite on the rate-setting committee for a 50 basis point move is limited. The bank said a hike of that size could signal that policy is well below where it needs to be and make the tightening cycle look open-ended. Its base case remains quarter-point hikes in December and March.

The detail behind the headline numbers explains the concern. Monthly core inflation edged down to 0.30% from 0.33%, but the three-month annualized pace rose to about 3.75%, from below 2% as recently as August. Excluding used cars, which fell 1.2%, core goods prices rose around 0.4%. Tariff-sensitive items such as toys, furniture and bedding, and appliances each rose more than 1%, and IT hardware prices climbed 0.4%. UBS noted that those categories carry larger weights in the Fed’s preferred PCE gauge than in CPI. It said goods disinflation looks a less reliable theme heading into 2027.

Shelter inflation slowed to 0.30% from 0.39% but remains sticky. Energy rose a further 0.7%, although its contribution to the headline figure faded. After two disappointing reports in a row, the December debate is now about the size of the move, not whether one comes.

The risk to this view is a messy or drawn-out leadership change, which would keep a discount on the stock and weigh on the AI-linked names that sold off alongside it. That includes Asian hardware suppliers with heavy Nvidia exposure.

---

Super Micro shows that scandal selling can overshoot, but Nvidia’s problem sits at the very top of the company, and that makes the parallel imperfect.

Summary:

  • The Wall Street Journal points to Super Micro Computer’s recovery as a possible sign Nvidia shares could rebound from the Huang turmoil
  • Super Micro co-founder Wally Liaw resigned from the board in March after being indicted over an alleged scheme to smuggle Nvidia-equipped servers to China
  • Super Micro shares plunged after his exit but have rebounded 48% from their March 20 low
  • Unlike Nvidia, Super Micro kept its CEO, so it faced no succession question
  • Nvidia’s next test is its results on November 17

Nvidia shareholders looking for a precedent may find one close to home. Super Micro Computer, which builds servers around Nvidia’s chips, went through its own China-linked scandal this year and has since staged a strong recovery. The Wall Street Journal suggests that pattern could point to an eventual rebound in Nvidia shares, despite the turmoil around chief executive Jensen Huang.

In March, federal prosecutors unsealed an indictment charging Super Micro co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw and two others with conspiring to divert about $2.5 billion of servers containing restricted Nvidia chips to China. Liaw resigned from the board, and Super Micro said it was cooperating with law enforcement. The shares plunged after his departure, but they have since climbed 48% from their March 20 low, the Journal noted.

The comparison has some logic. In both cases, the market’s first reaction was to price in the worst outcome. In Super Micro’s case, investors then reassessed once it became clear the underlying business was intact. Demand for AI hardware did not disappear because of a scandal at the top of a supplier. The same could prove true for Nvidia, whose chips remain the industry standard.

There are also important differences. Liaw was a director and senior executive, but Super Micro’s chief executive, Charles Liang, stayed in place, so the company kept its leadership. Nvidia’s problem centers on Huang himself, the co-founder whose vision and relationships with customers and governments are closely tied to the company’s identity. A forced exit would raise succession questions that Super Micro never faced. Nvidia is also far larger, so its recovery would depend on the broader AI trade as much as on relief specific to the stock.

Corporate history offers some reassurance. Several large companies, including Intel in 2018 and McDonald’s in 2019, lost chief executives over relationships with employees and carried on without lasting damage to the business. But neither was a founder-led firm at the center of a global technology race.

For now, the useful takeaway is that selling driven by scandal can overshoot when the business itself is sound. Whether that holds for Nvidia depends on what the board decides, how cleanly any succession is handled, and what the company says when it reports results on November 17.

The wider read-through is for crypto treasury companies. ---

  • Nvidia stock plunges after hours as New York Times reports new Jensen Huang relationship allegation
  • Nvidia CEO Huang faces 2nd relationship report as NYT links him to senior executive

---

MSCI has decided Strategy looks more like a bitcoin fund than a software company, and index trackers now have until November 30 to sell.

Summary:

  • MSCI will remove Strategy from its global indexes, including the MSCI USA Index, effective after the close on November 30
  • The decision is the first under MSCI’s new non-operating company rule, which screens operating assets and five financial ratios
  • Strategy went straight onto the deletion list, meaning it had already failed the two-year buffer for existing index members
  • Analysts estimated about $2.8 billion of passive selling, although that was calculated for MSCI’s earlier proposal
  • Strategy says trackers hold about 13 million shares, or 3.1% of its basic shares, and Saylor calls the rule discriminatory
  • Shares fell 0.8% after hours on Wednesday and are down about 20% this year

Strategy, the largest corporate holder of bitcoin, will be removed from MSCI’s global indexes after the index provider ruled that it more closely resembles an investment fund than an operating business. MSCI confirmed the deletion in its November index review on Wednesday. It takes effect after the close on November 30 and includes the flagship MSCI USA Index, according to Reuters and the published review list.

This is the first review under MSCI’s new non-operating company rule, which was finalised in mid-October. The rule first looks at a company’s operating assets and then tests it against five financial ratios. Companies that fail at least four of the five can be ruled ineligible. Existing index members generally have to fail across two annual reporting periods before they are removed. Strategy went straight onto the deletion list rather than the watch list, which means it had already used up that buffer.

The decision ends a reprieve that has lasted all year. In January, MSCI held back from excluding crypto treasury companies and promised a wider review of businesses whose main activity is holding assets. That review produced a deliberately asset-neutral test in August, but Strategy still failed it. A simulation using May data flagged Strategy, Japan’s Metaplanet and uranium holder Yellow Cake as deletions.

In practice, the removal forces selling by funds that track MSCI benchmarks. Analysts have estimated that selling at around $2.8 billion, although the figure was calculated for MSCI’s earlier crypto-specific proposal. Strategy has argued the impact will be modest. It says index trackers hold about 13 million shares, roughly 3.1% of its basic shares outstanding and less than a day’s typical trading volume. Executive chairman Michael Saylor has called the rule discriminatory and argues Strategy runs a genuine software business.

Strategy shares fell 0.8% in extended trading on Wednesday and are down about 20% this year, while bitcoin has lost about 15%. The bigger question is the longer term. Strategy funds its bitcoin buying largely by issuing shares, and losing part of its passive shareholder base could make that model more expensive, particularly if other index providers adopt similar rules.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.description:

NVDA shares reverse Wednesday's gains following a report that Nvidia's CEO had a relationship with an executive reporting to him. If confirmed, the allegations could add a new corporate-governance problem to the company's existing leadership controversy.

Nvidia (NVDA) shares are falling sharply in after-hours trading following a new report from The New York Times alleging that CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a company executive who reports to him.

According to a market quote captured at 00:11 GMT+2 on November 12, NVDA traded at $167.37 after hours, down $6.36 or 3.66% from Wednesday's regular-session close of $173.73.

The decline reverses more than Wednesday's 2.87% regular-session gain.

Why the latest Nvidia allegations matter to investors

The New York Times reported the new allegation late Wednesday, adding another potential complication for Nvidia's board of directors.

The company is already investigating Huang following earlier reports concerning his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence reportedly identified as having connections to Chinese intelligence.

That earlier controversy raised questions about national security, corporate oversight and whether sensitive information could have been compromised.

The latest allegation, however, introduces a potentially different concern.

If Huang had a relationship with an executive who reported directly to him, investors could reasonably question whether there were conflicts of interest involving management decisions, compensation, promotions or internal corporate governance.

A personal relationship does not, by itself, establish wrongdoing or improper conduct. The significance depends on the circumstances, the company's policies, what was disclosed to the board and whether any business decisions were affected.

The new allegation has not been independently verified by investingLive.

Why Nvidia stock could face additional pressure

Jensen Huang is not an ordinary corporate CEO. He co-founded Nvidia and has been central to its transformation into one of the world's most important artificial intelligence companies.

For shareholders, the concern is not simply the executive's personal conduct. It is whether repeated controversies could undermine confidence in Nvidia's leadership, distract management or increase pressure on its board.

There are three particularly important implications.

Corporate governance: Investors may demand clearer answers about how Nvidia's board oversees its CEO and manages potential conflicts of interest.

Leadership continuity: Any widening of the investigation could raise further questions about succession planning at a company closely associated with its founder.

Valuation and investor confidence: Even without changes to Nvidia's chip demand, earnings or competitive position, greater uncertainty about leadership could influence how much investors are willing to pay for the stock.

That does not mean Huang will leave Nvidia or that the allegations will ultimately affect the company's operations.

But investors may increasingly distinguish between confidence in Nvidia's AI business and confidence in its corporate leadership.

What NVDA traders should watch next

The immediate question is whether the after-hours selling continues when regular U.S. trading resumes Thursday, November 12.

The reported decline comes while the Nasdaq futures market is closed, limiting the ability to draw conclusions about the broader technology sector's reaction at that moment.

Traders should monitor whether Nvidia underperforms the Nasdaq and semiconductor stocks once futures trading resumes, and whether the company or its board responds to the latest reporting.

A recovery toward Wednesday's $173.73 closing price would suggest the initial selling is being absorbed. Sustained weakness would raise the possibility that investors are assigning a greater risk premium to Nvidia's leadership uncertainty.

For now, the market is reacting to another allegation rather than a confirmed finding of misconduct. What matters next is the evidence, the board's response and whether the situation begins to affect the company's ability to operate under its existing leadership.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nvidia CEO Huang faces 2nd relationship report as NYT links him to senior executive
item.description:
This shifts the Huang story from a national security question toward a corporate governance one, which is easier for investors to price and harder for the board to dismiss. A relationship with a direct report raises code-of-conduct issues, and it widens what the board’s investigation may need to examine. Huang is closely identified with Nvidia’s strategy and customer relationships, so any hint of leadership change would be a material risk for the stock. Because Nvidia is one of the S&P 500’s biggest weights, that risk reaches broad index exposure too. Expect the board review to compete with guidance for attention in next week’s results call, and headline-driven volatility around the November 17 results and the November 18 House briefing.

---

This is just turning into gossip magazine fodder now. Anyway, this is probably the final nail in Huang's coffin. 

Earlier:

  • Lutnick stalls Trump’s third Nvidia chip diversion crackdown this year, Axios says
  • Three risks for Nvidia shares after Huang admits affair with suspected Chinese spy

---

The Huang story is no longer only about China, and a relationship with a direct report puts Nvidia’s own code of conduct at the centre of the board’s review.

Summary:

  • The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s VP of health care, who reports to him, citing five people who worked at the company
  • Nvidia’s code of conduct tells staff to avoid conflicts, including personal relationships, and says it promptly investigates misconduct
  • The board is already investigating Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, whom US officials identified as a Chinese intelligence asset, with Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz leading the review
  • China denies the espionage claims, and Nvidia has said earlier allegations about Megaspeed diverting chips were debunked
  • Three House committee chairs have requested a closed-door briefing with Huang, reportedly on November 18
  • Nvidia reports third-quarter results on November 17

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of health care, who reports to him, The New York Times reported, citing five people who worked at the company. The relationship had not been reported before. It widens the scrutiny facing the head of the world’s leading AI chipmaker, less than a week before Nvidia reports quarterly results.

The report matters as a governance issue, not only a personal one. Nvidia’s code of conduct tells employees to avoid situations that create conflicts, including personal relationships, and says the company promptly investigates reports of misconduct. Many large companies bar managers from relationships with subordinates, because such ties can raise questions about pay, promotion and oversight. Both Huang and Powell are married to other people, according to the Times.

The new claim adds to an investigation already under way. Last month, the Times reported that US officials had identified Alice Huang as a Chinese intelligence asset. She is an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company, and had become close to the Nvidia CEO. She is no relation to Jensen Huang. After he acknowledged an affair with her, Nvidia’s board opened an investigation this month, led by the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. The board has said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. China has denied the espionage claims, and Alice Huang has not responded to requests for comment.

Nvidia has also pushed back on the wider allegations. It said earlier claims that Megaspeed diverted chips had been investigated and debunked last year, and Jensen Huang has described the company’s dealings with Megaspeed as normal.

Pressure is building in Washington too. The Republican chairs of three House committees have asked Huang to attend a closed-door briefing on his dealings with Alice Huang, reportedly on November 18. That is the day after Nvidia’s third-quarter results on November 17, when investors will be listening for any comment on the board’s review alongside the numbers. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and built it into the premier supplier of AI chips, which makes the question of how much the company depends on him an unusually sharp one for shareholders. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Lutnick stalls Trump’s third Nvidia chip diversion crackdown this year, Axios says
item.description:
For Nvidia, this adds another layer of policy uncertainty to a week already dominated by its board’s probe, and it keeps China-linked headline risk high heading into the requested House briefing. If enforcement tightens, it could weigh on sales routed through third-country buyers in Southeast Asia, although sales made through those channels are hard to size from public data. Nvidia is one of the heaviest weights in the S&P 500, so stock-specific shocks can move the wider index even when most other stocks are rising. Wall Street rebounded on Monday after the prior week’s selloff in AI stocks, but Nvidia fell, a sign that its own risks are now partly separate from the wider AI trade. A visible split between Bessent and Lutnick also matters beyond chips, because it raises questions about how consistently trade and export policy toward China will be applied.

---

Earlier:

  • Mizuho’s Klein calls Nvidia ‘silly cheap’ below 10x earnings despite Huang uncertainty
  • Morgans’ Stickley: S&P 500 up after every midterm since 1950 as Nvidia looks cheap

---

The White House wants to crack down on Nvidia chips leaking into China, but the department meant to enforce it is reportedly the one holding things up.

Summary:

  • Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has repeatedly stalled a crackdown on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China, Axios reported, citing high-level sources
  • Trump authorized the crackdown last Thursday, the third time this year, after consulting Elon Musk
  • In a Situation Room meeting with Bessent, Hegseth, Greer and Rubio, Bessent confronted Lutnick over his department’s resistance to enforcing the controls
  • Lutnick appeared to agree but said he needed to check with Trump, the report said
  • The report comes days after Nvidia’s board opened an independent probe into reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort

US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has repeatedly held up President Donald Trump’s crackdown on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia’s AI chips to China, Axios reported on Wednesday, citing high-level sources. The report reveals a split inside the administration over how hard to enforce export controls. It also comes while Nvidia is already facing heavy China-related scrutiny of its own.

According to Axios, Trump authorized the crackdown last Thursday after consulting Elon Musk. It was the third time this year he has done so. The same day, Lutnick met in the Situation Room with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Bessent challenged Lutnick over his department’s resistance to carrying out the controls. Lutnick appeared to agree but said he needed to check with Trump first, the report said.

Lutnick’s role matters because enforcement sits with the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, which licenses chip exports and polices diversion. A delay at Commerce can slow enforcement even after the White House has signed off. Diversion usually happens through buyers in third countries, often in Southeast Asian hubs such as Singapore, who resell restricted chips into China. In June, the bureau moved to close a loophole that may have let overseas units of Chinese companies obtain top-end Nvidia processors, according to Reuters.

The timing is awkward for Nvidia. On November 8, its board opened an independent investigation after reports that chief executive Jensen Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Independent directors are leading it, with help from outside counsel. The board said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised, and that it still has confidence in Huang. The New York Times reported that Megaspeed, a Singapore-based firm, bought about $4.8 billion of Nvidia chips over two years, although no wrongdoing by the company has been established. Nvidia shares fell about 4% on November 9, the first trading session after the board’s announcement.

Three Republican House committee chairs have reportedly asked for a closed-door briefing with Huang on November 18. For investors, the question is whether the Lutnick dispute ends in tougher, faster enforcement or a quieter compromise. Either way, Washington is now testing Nvidia’s China exposure from several directions at once.

Ahead:

  • Nvidia reports on Tuesday, 17 November, after the US close.
  • Nvidia will host a conference call on Tuesday, November 17, at 2 p.m. PT (5 p.m. ET) to discuss its financial results for the third quarter of fiscal year 2027, which ended October 25, 2026. That’s 22:00 GMT. Ahead of the call, Nvidia will provide written commentary from the CFO.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Anthropic IPO oversubscribed several times ahead of record $90 billion listing
item.description:
Raising close to $90 billion takes a lot of cash, and some fund managers may trim existing megacap tech holdings to make room, which could weigh on the Nasdaq as pricing approaches. Heavy oversubscription is a positive read-through for AI infrastructure stocks, especially the seven companies in the placement, because it shows public appetite for direct AI exposure remains strong. A strong first day would likely support the wider IPO pipeline, including OpenAI, which is reportedly aiming for 2027. A weak open would hit sentiment across AI-linked equities.

---

  • US stocks rally as AI shares rebound

---

Anthropic is heading into its debut with orders well ahead of supply, but the record-breaking $90 billion headline depends on pricing at the very top of the range.

Summary:

  • Anthropic’s IPO is already oversubscribed several times, driven by anchor-sized indications of interest, Bloomberg reported, citing unnamed sources
  • Shares are marketed at $70 to $78 each, implying a valuation of about $1.4 trillion, with trading expected to start next Thursday
  • The company is offering around 801 million Class A shares, and existing investors are selling roughly 24 million more
  • AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC have committed to buy $26 billion of Class N stock in a private placement
  • The combined target of about $90 billion would top SpaceX’s June record of about $86 billion including its over-allotment
  • CEO Dario Amodei will hold a live-streamed event with JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon on Friday

Anthropic’s initial public offering is already covered several times over, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter. That puts the Claude developer on course for what could be the largest stock market debut on record when its shares start trading next Thursday. The listing would make Anthropic the first major standalone frontier AI lab to go public.

According to the report, demand has been driven by indications of interest big enough to anchor the deal. In other words, individual investors are signalling orders large enough to underpin the whole book.

A filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on Tuesday set the price range at $70 to $78 a share, which would value the company at about $1.4 trillion. Anthropic is offering around 801 million Class A shares, and existing investors plan to sell roughly 24 million more. Separately, Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Google, Micron Technology, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC have committed to buy a combined $26 billion of Class N common stock through a private placement.

Together, the IPO and placement target about $90 billion. That would beat SpaceX’s June debut, which raised $75 billion in its base offering and about $86 billion once its over-allotment option was exercised. On the filing’s numbers, though, the $90 billion total assumes pricing at the top of the range. It also includes shares sold by existing holders, and that money goes to them, not to the company. At the bottom of the range, the combined total would be closer to $84 billion, short of SpaceX’s full raise.

The valuation is also a sharp step up from the private market. In June, Anthropic raised $65 billion at a $965 billion valuation, a round investors described as heavily oversubscribed, before filing confidentially for its listing. A $1.4 trillion valuation would be roughly 45% above that level.

To keep momentum going, chief executive Dario Amodei will hold a live-streamed event with JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon on Friday, the report said.

Final pricing will be the first real test of what public investors will pay for a frontier AI developer itself, not just the chipmakers and cloud providers that supply it. Seven of those suppliers are now also shareholders through the placement, which ties their fortunes more closely to Anthropic’s. Whether the deal prices at the top of the range, or gets bigger, will show how much of the private-market enthusiasm carries over. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Thursday, November 12, 2026 - low impact
item.description:
Its a low key day for the data agenda. The PPI data from Japan is of interest. 

Japan’s October producer price index (the corporate goods price index) is due at 23:50 GMT (18:50 US Eastern). Consensus looks for prices to rise 0.3% on the month, reversing September’s 0.3% drop. The annual rate is expected at 6.5%, down from 6.8%.

September’s figure missed forecasts. The annual rate slowed to 6.8% from 7.6% in August, mainly because of a 13.3% annual fall in agricultural prices as newly harvested rice got cheaper. An annual pace near 7% is still far above anything consistent with the BoJ’s price goal, though, so a softer October print would not mean pipeline pressure has gone away.

Three things to watch:

  1. Import prices. The yen-based import price index rose 24.5% year on year in September, or about 25%, with the weak yen still pushing up raw material costs. (Japan wholesale inflation misses at 6.8% but stays high enough to keep BOJ hike alive )
  2. Energy pass-through. Elevated oil prices linked to the Iran war magnify the effect of a weak yen on a country that imports most of its energy.
  3. Monthly momentum. If the month-on-month figure turns positive again, it would suggest the September dip was a blip and not the start of a turn lower.

BoJ implications

The BoJ held at 1.25% in an 8-1 vote on October 30, with Takata dissenting in favour of a hike to 1.5%. The board also raised its FY2027 inflation forecast to 2.6% from 2.4%. In a Bloomberg survey, 83% of economists expect the next hike in December, up from 35% a month earlier. The next policy meeting is on 17-18 December.

A print close to consensus is unlikely to change the December picture. A clear upside surprise would strengthen the hike case and could give the yen some support. A downside miss is unlikely to derail a hike, since the BoJ puts more weight on underlying consumer inflation and wages than on upstream goods prices.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
